description: Como docente, tengo el orgullo de presentar a StarMaker, un equipo conformado por estudiantes de segundo y tercer año de la Escuela Técnica Austral Petroleros Jerárquicos. Su nombre refleja exactamente lo que representan en el aula y en cada proyecto: jóvenes con el talento y la iniciativa para innovar, crear y destacar mediante la ciencia y la tecnología.
summary: HORIZON is a planetary research platform developed by Team Starmaker to identify and compare locations on Earth that share characteristics with regions of the Moon and Mars. Our research focused on five terrestrial locations and seven extraterrestrial regions, analyzing geology, topography, environmental conditions, gravity, radiation, and day length. We used information from NASA, other space agencies, and scientific publications to support our comparisons. Based on this research, we developed an interactive website that organizes scientific data, allows users to explore locations, visualize planetary metrics, compare environmental characteristics, and consult results and sources. HORIZON addresses the challenge by using Earth environments as reference points to better understand other worlds, identifying both similarities and differences. It is important because it makes scientific information more accessible, helps identify potential planetary analogues, and can support future research and space exploration mission planning.
details:
HORIZON

Technical Report: Research and Development Process

Team: Starmaker
Project: HORIZON
Competition: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Project Summary

HORIZON is the project developed by our team, Starmaker, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The challenge we selected was “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars.”

To address this challenge, we researched terrestrial locations with distinctive environmental, geological, and topographical characteristics. We investigated different climates, surface materials, landforms, and other conditions that could be compared with selected regions of Mars and the Moon.

After selecting five locations, we organized the collected information, examined their similarities and differences with planetary environments, and developed compatibility estimates. Finally, we brought the research together through HORIZON, an interactive website designed to make the information easier to explore and understand.

This report documents the research process, the decisions made by our team, the development of the platform, and the main findings of the project.

Main Stages

  1. Searching for and selecting potential terrestrial analogue sites.
  2. Collecting and organizing scientific information.
  3. Comparing the selected locations with Mars and the Moon.
  4. Evaluating similarities and developing compatibility estimates.
  5. Creating, reviewing, and improving the HORIZON website.
01. Introduction and Problem Statement

The Challenge That Led to HORIZON

HORIZON emerged from the NASA Space Apps Challenge, an international competition in which teams and individuals work on challenges related to science, technology, and space exploration.

Our team selected the challenge of identifying locations on Earth that could serve as analogues for environments relevant to permanent lunar bases and Mars.

The topic interested us because studying terrestrial environments can help us understand certain conditions that may be relevant to future space exploration. However, temperature alone cannot describe an entire environment. Two locations may have similar temperatures but completely different geological characteristics, precipitation levels, humidity, surface materials, or terrain.

For this reason, we expanded our investigation beyond temperature and considered several environmental and physical characteristics. Our goal was to develop comparisons based on documented information rather than relying only on photographs or visual similarities.

Research Question

Which locations on Earth share relevant characteristics with environments being considered for permanent lunar bases or with regions of Mars?

To answer this question, we selected terrestrial locations, gathered information about their characteristics, and compared them with selected planetary regions. We then organized the findings into compatibility estimates and presented the research through HORIZON.

General Objective

To identify and analyze five terrestrial locations by investigating their geological, topographical, and environmental characteristics, comparing them with selected regions of Mars and the Moon, and presenting the results through an interactive research platform.

Specific Objectives

  • Research terrestrial locations that could be relevant because of their environmental, geological, or terrain characteristics.
  • Compare the selected locations with regions of Mars and lunar environments of interest for permanent bases.
  • Identify similarities and differences between terrestrial and planetary environments.
  • Organize the collected information into comparable records.
  • Develop compatibility estimates based on the team's research.
  • Create a website that allows users to explore the locations, comparisons, results, and sources.

Scope of the Project

HORIZON focuses on researching and evaluating potential terrestrial analogue sites. The team did not take direct measurements on Mars or the Moon, nor did it conduct field measurements at every selected terrestrial location.

Instead, we consulted existing scientific and institutional sources and used the available information to investigate similarities between terrestrial environments and selected planetary regions.

The results represent the scope of our research and the criteria used by the team. They do not establish that any terrestrial location is an exact equivalent of Mars or the Moon.

02. Searching for and Selecting the Five Locations

Identifying Terrestrial Candidates

To address the challenge, our team searched for locations on Earth with characteristics that could be relevant to the study of lunar and Martian environments.

We considered different aspects of each environment, including geological features, landforms, climate, surface conditions, and the presence of water or ice.

Rather than selecting places based on a single characteristic, we aimed to build a diverse group of candidates. This allowed us to investigate different types of terrestrial environments and evaluate which of their documented characteristics could be compared with regions of the Moon and Mars.

The Five Selected Locations

These locations were selected as research candidates, not as confirmed equivalents of lunar or Martian environments. Each one offers different characteristics that can be investigated, but not every characteristic necessarily represents a similarity with another planetary body.

Why We Selected Different Types of Environments

Selecting locations from different geographical and geological settings allowed us to examine a wider range of characteristics.

For example, Changthang provides a reference for studying high-altitude arid environments, while La Quemada de Órzola offers volcanic landforms and basaltic surfaces.

Other locations, such as Grüner See, Lake Winnipesaukee, and Walchensee, provide examples of environments shaped by water, glacial processes, seasonal changes, or mountainous terrain.

This diversity was important because the challenge was not simply to find landscapes that looked similar to Mars or the Moon. We wanted to investigate specific characteristics, identify possible similarities, and recognize the differences that limit each comparison.

The selection stage therefore established the five terrestrial sites that would be documented and evaluated throughout the project.

03. Collecting and Organizing Information

From Location Selection to Scientific Information

After selecting the five terrestrial locations, we gathered and organized information about their geographical, geological, and environmental characteristics.

The purpose was to create comparable profiles for each site. Instead of relying only on visual similarities, we considered documented information about the environments and their physical characteristics.

The research included several dimensions:

  • Geological characteristics and surface materials.
  • Topography and landforms.
  • Environmental conditions, including aridity and water availability.
  • Thermal characteristics, where reliable information was available.
  • Operational considerations related to the possible usefulness of the terrain for exploration.

These dimensions helped us organize the information and identify which aspects could be compared with the Moon and Mars.

Geological Characteristics and Surface Materials

Geological information was important for understanding the materials and processes that shape each terrestrial location.

For example, La Quemada de Órzola contains a basaltic pyroclastic cone and rough lava flows, known locally as malpaís. These features make it relevant to comparisons involving volcanic surfaces and basaltic landforms.

Other locations provide different geological contexts. Changthang includes high-altitude environments and saline lakes, while Lake Winnipesaukee is associated with a glacial landscape over crystalline bedrock.

Studying these differences allowed us to consider whether the geological characteristics of a terrestrial site could provide a useful reference for understanding certain planetary environments.

Topography and Landforms

We also examined the physical shape of each landscape. This included features such as volcanic cones, lava fields, mountainous terrain, lake basins, and other surface formations.

Topography matters because the shape and roughness of a surface can influence mobility, navigation, geological interpretation, and the planning of exploration activities.

In HORIZON, topographical characteristics are one of the dimensions used to evaluate similarities between terrestrial sites and planetary reference regions.

Environmental Conditions and Water

Environmental information was another important part of the research. We considered characteristics such as aridity, the presence of surface water, and seasonal environmental changes.

For example, Changthang is a high-altitude cold desert with saline lakes and hydrothermal environments. Grüner See is a karst lake whose water level rises during spring due to snowmelt. La Quemada de Órzola, in contrast, is characterized by an arid climate and sparse vegetation.

These examples show why the presence or absence of water must be interpreted carefully. Liquid water in a terrestrial lake does not represent the same conditions as possible subsurface ice or ancient water-related environments on Mars, nor does it reproduce the conditions of the lunar surface.

Thermal Information and Data Limitations

Temperature was considered as part of the broader environmental investigation. However, the availability of comparable thermal information varies between locations.

When comparing temperatures, it is important to distinguish between typical values, maximum and minimum temperatures, seasonal changes, and isolated measurements. These values cannot be treated as equivalent without considering their context and reference periods.

Where comparable information was insufficient, we avoided treating the absence of data as evidence of environmental incompatibility.

Organizing the Information in HORIZON

To make the research easier to consult, we organized information into records for the terrestrial sites and planetary regions.

The current platform brings together:

  • 36 research records.
  • 5 terrestrial locations.
  • 7 planetary reference regions.
  • 24 sources.

The information is organized so that users can consult the characteristics of each location, review planetary regions, examine comparison results, and access the references used in the project.

04. Comparison with Mars and the Moon

Comparing Terrestrial Sites with Planetary Regions

A central part of HORIZON is the comparison between the five terrestrial locations and selected regions of Mars and the Moon.

We did not treat Mars and the Moon as interchangeable environments. Each has different geological, physical, and environmental conditions, so the comparison needs to consider the characteristics relevant to each planetary region.

The platform includes seven planetary reference regions: four on Mars and three on the Moon.

These regions provide different geological and environmental contexts for the comparisons.

Comparison with Mars

For Mars, HORIZON includes regions associated with ancient water-related environments, periglacial terrain, subsurface ice, and volcanic landforms.

For example, Jezero Crater is relevant because of evidence for an ancient lake environment and possible lacustrine minerals. Gale Crater contains evidence of an ancient fluvial-lacustrine environment. Utopia Planitia provides a reference for studying periglacial terrain and possible subsurface ice, while Tharsis Montes represents a major volcanic region.

The terrestrial sites can be compared with these regions through specific characteristics, such as surface materials, landforms, and environmental conditions.

Comparison with Lunar Environments

The lunar comparison includes Mare Tranquillitatis, Marius Hills, and Shackleton Crater.

These regions were selected because they represent different lunar characteristics. Mare Tranquillitatis and Marius Hills are associated with basaltic volcanic terrain, while Shackleton Crater is important for studying permanently shadowed regions and the possibility of water ice near the lunar south pole.

The comparison with terrestrial sites is based on specific characteristics rather than complete environmental equivalence.

Earth has an atmosphere, liquid water, and a different gravitational and radiation environment. The Moon does not have an atmosphere comparable to Earth's, and its surface experiences conditions that cannot be fully reproduced at any terrestrial location.

Why Differences Are Important

A useful comparison must identify differences as well as similarities.

A terrestrial location may share certain landforms or environmental characteristics with a planetary region while differing significantly in its geological composition, atmosphere, water conditions, or radiation exposure.

HORIZON therefore considers limitations alongside similarities. This helps prevent the results from being interpreted as proof that a terrestrial location is identical to Mars or the Moon.

05. Evaluation Method and Development of the Ranking

Comparing Compatibility with Mars and the Moon

After organizing the information and comparing the terrestrial sites with the planetary reference regions, we evaluated the degree of similarity between the selected environments.

The comparison with Mars and the comparison with the Moon were treated separately. This distinction is important because a terrestrial location may share more characteristics with one planetary body than with the other.

One of the main findings from our research was the compatibility identified for Changthang:

Terrestrial location

Mars compatibility

Moon compatibility

Changthang

62%

31%

According to the data collected and analyzed by our team, Changthang showed its strongest compatibility with Mars, reaching 62%, while its compatibility with the Moon was 31%.

These percentages represent the results of our team's comparison and should be interpreted within the scope of the selected criteria and available information. They are not official NASA classifications or universal scientific measurements.

Criteria Considered

The research considered several characteristics when comparing terrestrial and planetary environments:

  • Temperature and thermal conditions.
  • Climate and environmental characteristics.
  • Geological composition and surface materials.
  • Topography and landforms.
  • Water, ice, and related environmental features.

The relevance of each characteristic depends on the planetary region being considered. For example, basaltic surfaces are relevant when comparing volcanic terrain, while aridity and environmental conditions may be more relevant in other comparisons.

Interpreting the Results

The results indicate that Changthang presented a stronger similarity with Mars than with the Moon within the comparisons conducted by our team.

Its 62% Mars compatibility and 31% lunar compatibility illustrate why the two comparisons must remain separate. A location can be a more relevant analogue for one planetary environment without necessarily being equally compatible with another.

The percentages should not be interpreted as proof that Changthang reproduces the complete environment of Mars or the Moon. They summarize the similarities identified through the project's research and criteria.

A complete explanation of the calculation procedure, including the original records and any weighting applied, is important for making the results reproducible.

06. Development of the HORIZON Website

Turning the Research into an Interactive Platform

After researching the terrestrial sites and planetary regions, we developed HORIZON as a digital platform to organize and present the project's information.

The website was created to make the research easier to explore than a traditional report containing long sections of text. It brings together site profiles, planetary references, comparison results, metrics, and scientific sources in one place.

HORIZON is presented as a planetary research platform under the idea that planetary investigation can begin by studying environments on Earth.

Main Sections of the Website

The current version of HORIZON includes six main sections:

  • Explore: Presents the terrestrial locations and their documented characteristics.
  • Compare: Provides access to the comparison between terrestrial sites and planetary environments.
  • Analogues: Presents the similarities, differences, and limitations identified in the research.
  • Metrics: Explains four physical metrics relevant to planetary exploration: gravity, escape velocity, radiation, and day length.
  • Results: Displays the project's comparison findings and compatibility information.
  • Library: Organizes the scientific references and data sources used by the project.

The platform also includes a language selector and organizes the research into a sequence that goes from selecting a terrestrial site to presenting a planetary comparison and conclusion.

Four Physical Metrics Relevant to Planetary Exploration

In addition to the site comparisons, HORIZON includes a separate section explaining four physical metrics that influence exploration on Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

1. Gravity

Gravity affects mobility, traction, vehicles, instruments, and movement across the surface. Lunar gravity is approximately one-sixth of Earth's, while Martian gravity is approximately 38% of Earth's.

2. Escape Velocity

Escape velocity represents the minimum ideal speed required to escape a body's gravitational field. It is relevant to understanding ascent and propulsion requirements.

3. Radiation

The website presents surface radiation information using measurements from specific sources and locations. The lunar data are associated with the Chang'e-4 LND instrument, while the Martian data come from the Curiosity rover's RAD instrument in Gale Crater.

These measurements refer to specific locations and periods rather than universal values for the entire planetary surface.

4. Day Length

Day length affects lighting cycles, energy availability, and mission planning. The lunar surface experiences long periods of daylight and darkness, while a Martian solar day is approximately 1.03 Earth days.

These metrics provide context for the physical challenges of planetary exploration. They are not direct measurements taken at the five terrestrial sites and are not presented as the sole basis for the compatibility comparisons.

Presenting Scientific Information Clearly

One of the main goals of the website is to make the information understandable without removing its scientific context.

For this reason, HORIZON presents not only comparison results but also the characteristics behind the research, the limitations of the available data, and the sources used.

The website is intended to function as an organized way to explore the research and understand how the team reached its conclusions.

07. Review, Redesign, and Current Improvements

Reviewing the Platform

During development, we reviewed the way the information was organized and presented. This process helped us identify where explanations needed to be clearer and where the separation between site descriptions, planetary comparisons, metrics, and results could be improved.

The current published version is HORIZON 3.0. It brings the main research sections together and presents the five terrestrial sites, seven planetary regions, comparison dimensions, research results, and scientific library.

Areas for Improvement

Although the platform already presents the project's main information, there are areas that could be improved in future versions:

  • Provide a more detailed explanation of the mathematical procedure behind the compatibility percentages.
  • Include additional comparable thermal measurements for the terrestrial sites.
  • Expand the documentation supporting each comparison.
  • Verify secondary references using institutional or primary sources.
  • Improve the explanation of confidence labels and missing data.
  • Add further measurements and observations when reliable information becomes available.

These improvements would make the results easier to reproduce, interpret, and evaluate.

What We Learned from Reviewing the Website

Developing and reviewing HORIZON showed us that scientific research and communicating scientific information are related but different tasks.

Research requires collecting and checking information, identifying relevant characteristics, and recognizing limitations. Presenting that research requires organizing the results so that other people can understand what was compared and what the conclusions actually mean.

The development process helped us connect these two tasks through an interactive platform.

08. Importance, Limitations, and Possibilities of the Project

Why Studying Terrestrial Environments Is Useful

Terrestrial analogue research can help scientists investigate selected characteristics of environments that are relevant to planetary exploration.

A location on Earth cannot reproduce all the conditions of Mars or the Moon. However, it may provide a useful reference for studying particular geological features, landforms, environmental conditions, or exploration challenges.

HORIZON applies this idea by organizing information about five terrestrial locations and comparing their documented characteristics with selected regions of Mars and the Moon.

The project's contribution is to bring together information from different sources, organize it through common comparison dimensions, and present the results in an accessible digital platform.

Limitations of the Research

There are several limitations that must be considered when interpreting HORIZON's results.

First, the project relies on existing sources and records. The team did not conduct direct field measurements at all five terrestrial locations. Consequently, the quality of the comparisons depends on the availability, reliability, and comparability of the information consulted.

Second, not every dimension has sufficient data. Some characteristics require additional measurements or more comparable records before they can be evaluated consistently.

Third, terrestrial environments cannot reproduce the complete physical conditions of the Moon or Mars. Differences in gravity, radiation, atmospheric pressure, and day length remain important even when certain surface characteristics are similar.

Finally, compatibility percentages must be interpreted within the scope of the project's comparison system. A complete explanation of the calculation method would improve transparency and reproducibility.

Future Possibilities

HORIZON can be expanded through additional research and improved documentation.

Possible next steps include collecting more comparable temperature and surface measurements, verifying secondary sources with institutional records, expanding the number of terrestrial sites, and improving the explanation of the scoring procedure.

Further research could also include in-situ measurements of surface temperature, slope, and illumination, field spectroscopy that can be compared with orbital data, and the study of SAR and optical image time series to examine seasonal variations.

These are proposed research directions, not measurements or analyses that the team claims to have already completed.

09. Conclusion and Pending Documentation

Conclusion

HORIZON was developed by our team, Starmaker, as a response to a planetary research challenge. The project focuses on identifying and evaluating terrestrial environments that share selected characteristics with regions of the Moon and Mars.

We selected five locations: Changthang in Ladakh, India; Grüner See in Austria; Lake Winnipesaukee in the United States; La Quemada de Órzola in Lanzarote, Spain; and Walchensee in Germany.

We gathered and organized information about their geological, topographical, and environmental characteristics. We then compared these locations with seven planetary reference regions: Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Utopia Planitia, and Tharsis Montes on Mars; and Mare Tranquillitatis, Marius Hills, and Shackleton Crater on the Moon.

One of the important findings of our research was Changthang's compatibility with Mars and the Moon. Based on our team's comparison, Changthang reached 62% compatibility with Mars and 31% with the Moon. This showed a stronger relationship with the Martian environment within the criteria and data considered in our research.

We also developed HORIZON as an interactive website to bring the research together. Its sections allow users to explore terrestrial sites, examine planetary regions, consult physical metrics, review comparison results, and access scientific sources.

Through this project, we learned how to approach a scientific challenge, investigate different environments, organize information, compare characteristics, recognize limitations, and communicate research through a digital platform.

HORIZON represents our effort to connect Earth-based research with the study of other worlds and to make planetary analogue research more accessible.
